text: Cloud Security Posture Management gets described with a lot of marketing language, but strip that away and the mechanism is simple: a CSPM tool continuously reads your real cloud configuration through the same APIs you'd use yourself, compares it against a library of known-good rules, and flags any mismatch as a finding. Microsoft Defender for Cloud and AWS Security Hub are both CSPM tools in exactly this sense.

Defender for Cloud's secure score isn't one opaque number. It's a weighted aggregate of individual security controls, each one scored as the ratio of healthy resources to total applicable resources, multiplied by that control's point weight. A control about securing SQL databases contributes zero points if you don't have any SQL databases deployed — that's not a penalty, it's just not relevant to your environment. Reading which controls are missing points matters far more than watching one percentage move.

AWS Security Hub takes a different shape. Instead of one blended score, it aggregates findings from its own automated checks plus services like GuardDuty and Inspector into a normalized format, and shows a pass or fail percentage per enabled standard — the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, or the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard — scored independently rather than combined into a single number.

Here's the distinction that separates engineers who just watch a dashboard from engineers who use one well. CSPM tells you configuration state, right now — is this resource compliant with this specific rule. It does not tell you whether an attacker is already inside your environment; that's threat detection's job, not posture management's. And a 100% compliant standard only means your checked configuration surface is clean — it says nothing about a misconfiguration the rule set doesn't test for, or a legitimate credential already being misused.

CSPM is necessary — you can't manage what you don't continuously measure — but it's one input into a security program, not the whole program. That closes this chapter: you can now place the responsibility line correctly, treat two clouds as one program with two implementations, build a real baseline from CIS Benchmarks, and read what a posture score is actually built from underneath. Chapter 2 moves from measuring posture to engineering the identity layer those controls depend on.
